fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Wu Wei as the Most Appropriate Action", "body": "Gregory Ripley pushes back on translating wu wei flatly as non action. He tells Chance Garton it is closer to the most efficient, effective or appropriate response to whatever is in front of you, the same way planets spin through galaxies without volition or a sense of self. He traces it back to his own Tai Chi and push hands training, where doing it correctly feels like you did nothing at all, and to years working alone in a coffee shop, where moving smoothly through a rush made the line disappear. Problems still arrive, they just stop feeling like problems."}, {"title": "Precepts Reframed as Medicine", "body": "The Hundred Remedies of the Tao, out from Inner Traditions on December 5th, translates a precepts text from roughly the fifth or sixth century. Ripley explains that what makes it unusual is the framing. The Chinese character is yao, the same word used for an herbal remedy in Chinese medicine, so each entry reads as a medicine rather than a thou shalt. He links this to Zen texts about diseases of the mind and to the Medicine Buddha as spiritual physician. Chance connects it to his own energy work, focused on limiting beliefs, which he sees as blocking the flow of life force and eventually surfacing as disease."}, {"title": "Star Lords, the Dipper, and the Still Point", "body": "Chance raises the seven stars of Ursa Major envisioned as Star Lords, and the pole star as the one fixed point everything revolves around. Ripley agrees, citing a line from Confucius about the virtuous ruler sitting still while the world turns around him, and says finding that still point within yourself is the inner match for the north star. He describes Daoist ritual as largely untranslated in the West, mentions a teacher currently in China spending a month on Quanzhen precept ceremonies, and points to the Beidou Jing, the Northern Dipper scripture, and birthday practices tied to your governing star."}, {"title": "Phonetic Bridges Between East and West", "body": "Chance runs a philological thread through the whole conversation. Yao for medicine echoes the Greek IAO, iota alpha omega, an ancient name for the Supreme Being. Tian, the sky or heavens, and Tian Di, the Heavenly Father, echo the Etruscan Tinia and the Latin root for god behind Jupiter and Zeus. In the outro he adds Shin, the Chinese suffix for mental and spiritual activity, the Japanese shin meaning true or heart, the Hebrew letter of fire, and the Latin san behind sanctity and health. Ripley grants the sound connections are striking while noting the characters would need separate study."}, {"title": "Nature Connection and the Unmediated Experience", "body": "Ripley also guides forest therapy, which grew out of the Japanese practice of shinrin yoku, coined in the early eighties by the head of the forestry department there. His acupuncture practice convinced him many complaints came from unnatural rhythms of sleeping, waking and eating, and MovNat style natural movement pulled him further that way. His guiding principle is that the guide opens the doors but the forest is the therapist. Chance ties this to plant blindness, to a moment he suddenly saw every distinct shade of green, and to Baudrillard on hyper reality, where our labels replace the thing itself."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Gregory Ripley is a Taoist Priest in the Quanzhen Longmen tradition, and a Forest Therapy Guide. In this episode we discuss his brand new book, One Hundred Remedies of the Tao: Spiritual Wisdom for Interesting Times. Throughout this conversation we discuss Wu Wei and achieving "the zone" flow states, how philosophy acts as medicine, syncretism between the mystery schools of ancient far east and Occident, the role of luminaries and the pole star in Taoism, and much more.
fields.Intro Paragraph 2: In the Plus+ Extension, we investigate the relationship of the living to their ancestors, the primordial being Pangu, dynastic cycles as world age revolutions, the emperor as sacred center, eclipses and the saving of the sun ritual, Mercury and internal alchemy, and how to keep hold of our spiritual epiphanies in times of dissonance.

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Ancestors Honored in the Heart", "body": "Chance reads a passage from the book promising that chanting a scripture ten times saves myriad generations of ancestors, who ascend to the Vermilion Palace. Gregory explains that Daoist images of many hells were heavily influenced by Buddhism, while Laozi and Zhuangzi reflect older ideas about natural cycles of life and death. His own reading treats the Vermilion or Crimson Palace as a name for the heart, so ancestors we honor there become honored beings. He adds that buried injustices keep haunting cultures and individuals until they are faced, and describes a novel that felt narrated to him."}, {"title": "Pangu, Lawgivers and the Sacred Center", "body": "Asked about a firstborn being like Manu or Phanes, Gregory names Pangu, whose eyes echo the sun and moon and whose body becomes mountain ranges, then the Three Pure Ones, with Daode Tianzun linked to Laozi. Huangdi, the Yellow Emperor, stands as first ancestor and giver of culture, while Chance traces Manu through Minos and the Aztec Yellow Woman. Gregory ties world ages to the dynastic cycle and the Mandate of Heaven. Chance recalls units of measure being reset to each new ruler, and Gregory notes acupuncture's cun is scaled to each body."}, {"title": "The Dantian and Mercurial Alchemy", "body": "Gregory introduces the three dantians of belly, chest and head, with the lower one as the body's battery or furnace, noting that some schools say everyone is born with it and others say it must be built. Focusing there deepens the breath and calms the nervous system, while esoterically it gathers energy for cultivation. Dan means cinnabar or elixir, and Chance links cinnabar to mercury and internal alchemy over any physical philosopher's stone. Gregory reframes mercurial as a positive, formless adaptability, and Chance's farmer parable, which Gregory traces to the Huainanzi, shows fortune turning endlessly."}, {"title": "Yu Wei, Service and Healthy Selfhood", "body": "Gregory describes yu wei as deliberate, effortful action, like a basketball player's lifetime of drills that makes flow possible, and outlines two models of internal alchemy, a return to original naturalness and gradual cultivation. Chance warns against self-sacrificing service done for recognition, favoring gifts shared from abundance, and calls the Western savior complex a psychological operation that undermines self-reliance. Gregory sees activists burning out through the same pattern and recalls a teacher who advised helping whoever is in front of you without meddling. He argues a healthy ego is needed, since total egolessness makes a person a doormat."}, {"title": "Eclipses, Maybe and Keeping Epiphanies", "body": "Gregory compares the ritual of banging drums to save the sun from a devouring celestial dog or wolf to a protest rally, a warning to rulers straying from the Mandate of Heaven, and stresses the old duty of honest advisors. Chance links the wolf to Ragnarok. Gregory returns to a teacher's call to rest in maybe rather than judgment. Chance asks how to hold on to epiphanies we keep losing, and Gregory suggests rereading texts that carry them and names xin dao, trust in the Dao that also means a clear signal path. Chance suggests pinning epiphanies up on Post-It notes."}]

fields.Plus Quotes JSON: [{"text": "I think it may be that there are times when we almost kind of download information from the universe.", "author": "Gregory Ripley", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/123c1d6c-5d5b-4ecf-a3b8-e8f68b7a900b/GREGORY-RIPLEY.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "The emperor, of course, is the center of the universe in terms of the culture and the civilization and the laws and everything.", "author": "Gregory Ripley", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/123c1d6c-5d5b-4ecf-a3b8-e8f68b7a900b/GREGORY-RIPLEY.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "The trickster element of these mercurial archetypes is such that you can expect this character or this aspect of life to bring good where there's bad and to bring bad where there's good.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "We practice in meditation or spirituality, or these different modalities, we practice very consciously for a long time for those moments of non-action.", "author": "Gregory Ripley", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/123c1d6c-5d5b-4ecf-a3b8-e8f68b7a900b/GREGORY-RIPLEY.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "If everybody sacrifices themself for everybody, then everybody is sacrificed.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "You need to have a healthy level of ego. You can't be completely egoless because then you could just become a doormat.", "author": "Gregory Ripley", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/123c1d6c-5d5b-4ecf-a3b8-e8f68b7a900b/GREGORY-RIPLEY.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "The most destructive egos I've found are the ones that are most angered into victimization and feeling like things are being done to them.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "Did you peak in high school and it's all downhill from there? Or are you going to peak when you're 90?", "author": "Gregory Ripley", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/123c1d6c-5d5b-4ecf-a3b8-e8f68b7a900b/GREGORY-RIPLEY.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "This is a thought-based universe, and the right thoughts can spiral you into despair or lift you into bliss.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "Just try to take life a little more easily. Let it come as it comes and let it go as it goes.", "author": "Gregory Ripley", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/123c1d6c-5d5b-4ecf-a3b8-e8f68b7a900b/GREGORY-RIPLEY.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}]
fields.Quotes JSON: [{"text": "And so it just seemed like a theme this month for me to be just digging into the ways that we can heal ourselves within and without, including our our world by more harmonious ways of thinking and being in the world.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "And then you get a sense where you kind of start to lose a sense of where your skin ends and the rest of the world begins, you know? And I suppose it's in Western terms, it's probably something akin to a unity consciousness or something like that.", "author": "Gregory Ripley", "portrait": ""}, {"text": "They don't seem like problems. It's like, this is just what's happening. You deal with it in the moment. You move on to the next moment and do what's most appropriate, you know, moment, moment to moment.", "author": "Gregory Ripley", "portrait": ""}, {"text": "And, and this is kind of saying, Hey, you know, this isn't necessarily like some hard and fast rule.
